Several open-source CLIs fit this description. The strongest matches are:

- **leakguard** (Rust): It reads stdin or files and writes redacted text to stdout. It covers emails, IPs, JWTs, and API keys, and a `--check` mode exits non-zero when sensitive data is found. Fast, zero-dependency redaction of secrets and PII (emails, credit cards, IPs, JWTs, API keys, and more) from text and logs.
- **local-redact** (Python): This one is built for the LLM use case. It is pitched as a way to Redact sensitive data before you paste it into an LLM. It handles stdin-to-stdout, a JSON report, and restoring answers afterward. Its detectors include IP addresses and API keys. It also covers regional IDs, which matter less for logs.
- **hexredact** (CLI for logs): It reads stdin with `-` and writes clean text to stdout. It uses reversible tokens, so the same IP always maps to the same token. The same value always gets the same token, so you can still follow one IP or user through the logs. Its stdout-only design fits piping.
- **cleansh** (Rust): It is aimed at terminal output. It covers emails, IPv4 and IPv6, and tokens such as JWTs, AWS, and GCP keys. Its docs show piping from `docker logs` and `kubectl logs`.
- **rog7/redact** (Python): This is a simpler option. It hides emails, API keys, and tokens, and it prints the cleaned log to stdout without modifying the original file.

For LLM sharing, local-redact and hexredact are the strongest fits. local-redact handles the restore step, and hexredact keeps relationships between values intact. leakguard and cleansh are good for plain stdin filtering. I did not check the licenses, maintenance status, or current versions of any of these, so verify those before adopting one.

content.content:
**leakguard 1.0.0** is a Rust library and CLI that finds and removes secrets and personal data (PII) from text and logs. It has no dependencies, and its docs describe it as "Fast, zero-dependency redaction of secrets and PII" from text and logs.

- **License:** Dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0, at your option.
- **Release date:** 2026-10-06.
- **Repository:** https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard
- **Install:**
  - Library: add `leakguard = "1.0.0"` to `[dependencies]` in `Cargo.toml`.
  - CLI: run `cargo install leakguard`.
- **Usage (stdin/stdout):**
  - Pipe a live log through it: `tail -f app.log | leakguard`
  - Redact a file to stdout, keeping the last 4 characters: `leakguard --mask partial --keep 4 access.log > clean.log`
  - Library example: an email address and an IPv4 address in a sentence are replaced with labels such as `[REDACTED:EMAIL]` and `[REDACTED:IPV4]`.
- **Detects:** Email addresses, credit card numbers (Luhn-validated), IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, US SSNs, MAC addresses, IBANs (checksum-validated), URLs with embedded credentials, private keys, and API tokens from providers such as AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google, OpenAI, Azure, Telegram, and Discord. Phone numbers and high-entropy strings are opt-in because they produce more false positives. Custom detectors are also supported.

The docs call it a best-effort tool, not a complete solution, and note that some secrets may go undetected and some detections may be false positives.

content.content:
**CleanSH (cleansh)** is a command-line tool that redacts sensitive data from terminal output so it can be shared safely. It reads from stdin or files, and it works with a pre-configured set of rules.

- **Latest version:** 0.1.11 (released 2025-12-20)
- **License:** The CLI and core library are "Licensed under **MIT OR Apache-2.0**." The earlier PolyForm license no longer applies to v0.1.9 and later.
- **Install:** `cargo install cleansh`. Prebuilt binaries are also available from GitHub Releases.
- **Usage (stdin/stdout):** Pipe text into it, for example `echo "My email is test@example.com" | cleansh sanitize`. The page shows this pattern with `docker logs` and `git config --list`, but it doesn't spell out the output behavior in detail.
- **Detects:**
  - Emails and IPv4/IPv6 addresses
  - Tokens and secrets: JWTs, GitHub PATs, Stripe keys, AWS/GCP/Azure keys, SSH keys, and generic hex tokens
  - PII: credit cards, US SSNs, UK NINOs, and South African IDs
  - File paths, such as `/home/user` becoming `~/`
  - Optional entropy-based detection for secrets without a known format, enabled with `--engine entropy`
- **Repository:** https://github.com/KarmaYama/cleansh-workspace
- **Telemetry/network:** The page doesn't mention telemetry. It does list `reqwest` as a dependency, but it doesn't say what that's used for. The page also says the planned `cleansh profiles sync` feature is an "inactive stub" in the open-source CLI.

content.text:
I recommend **leakguard**. It's a small Rust command-line tool that reads stdin and writes the redacted text to stdout. It runs entirely on your machine, the regexes are built in, and it's free (MIT or Apache-2.0).

## Main recommendation: leakguard

- **Repo:** https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard. Version 1.0.0 came out on 2026-10-06.
- **What it catches by default:** email addresses, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, private keys, URLs with a username and password in them, and API tokens from AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google, OpenAI, Azure, Telegram and Discord. It also catches credit card numbers, IBANs, US Social Security numbers and MAC addresses.
- **Off by default:** phone numbers and "high-entropy" strings (random-looking values that might be secrets). You can turn them on, but they flag more things that aren't secrets.
- **Output:** each match is replaced with a label, such as `[REDACTED:EMAIL]` or `[REDACTED:IPV4]`.

### Install
I'm assuming you don't have a Rust toolchain yet and that no prebuilt Linux binary is available. If the repo's Releases page has one, you can use that instead.
```bash
# 1. Install Rust (skip if `cargo --version` already works)
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source "$HOME/.cargo/env"

# 2. Install leakguard
cargo install leakguard
leakguard --help
```

### First run
```bash
# Check it on fake data first
printf 'user bob@example.com from 203.0.113.7 token ghp_%s\n' "$(head -c 36 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')" | leakguard

# Redact a log file to a new file, then read the result before pasting it
leakguard app.log > app.clean.log
less app.clean.log

# Or pipe logs straight in
journalctl -u myservice --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > clean.log

# Keep the last 4 characters of each match, so you can still tell values apart
leakguard --mask partial --keep 4 access.log > clean.log
```
If you use X11 and want the redacted text on your clipboard, pipe it on with `... | leakguard | xclip -selection clipboard`.

## Alternatives
- **cleansh** ([KarmaYama/cleansh-workspace](https://github.com/KarmaYama/cleansh-workspace), MIT or Apache-2.0). Install with `cargo install cleansh`, then run `docker logs x | cleansh sanitize`. It covers similar ground, can also shorten home-directory paths to `~/`, and has an optional entropy mode for secrets that don't match a known pattern. One thing to check: it lists an HTTP library among its dependencies, and its docs don't say what that's for.
- **hexredact** ([happygream/hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)). It replaces each value with a token, and the same value always gets the same token. That means you can still follow one IP or user through the logs.
- **local-redact** ([sumankrsh/local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)). It's built specifically for pasting into an LLM and can put the original values back into the answer afterwards.
- **rog7/redact** ([GitHub](https://github.com/rog7/redact)). A simpler Python script that hides emails, API keys and tokens.

## Caveats
- **Pattern matching misses things.** leakguard's own docs call it "best-effort." It won't catch internal hostnames, usernames, customer IDs or home-grown token formats. Always skim the output before you paste it.
- **For more coverage, turn on the extra checks.** The high-entropy option (or cleansh's entropy mode) catches random-looking secrets that don't match a known format.
- **These are small projects run by individuals.** I didn't review their code, so look at the repo, or build from a specific tagged release, before trusting one with production logs.

Sources:
- [leakguard on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest)
- [leakguard source](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [cleansh on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/cleansh/latest)
- [cleansh crate docs](https://docs.rs/cleansh/0.1.7/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/cleansh/)
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
- [pncli PR #504](https://github.com/kolatts/pncli/pull/504)
